title: Immune 'reprogramming' could protect poultry from deadly diseases without antibiotics
excerpt: University of Bristol–led researchers have identified a naturally occurring gut molecule that could strengthen chickens' immune response against a wide range of bacterial infections. This development, published today, Aug. 12, in The Journal of Immunology, offers a major step forward in sustainable farming and the global fight against antibiotic resistance.
content_html:
University of Bristol–led researchers have identified a naturally occurring gut molecule that could strengthen chickens' immune response against a wide range of bacterial infections. This development, published today, Aug. 12, in The Journal of Immunology, offers a major step forward in sustainable farming and the global fight against antibiotic resistance.

It has long been a challenge in agriculture to protect livestock from widespread pathogens such as Salmonella and avian pathogenic E. coli (APEC) without relying heavily on antibiotics. Overuse of these drugs in farming contributes directly to the global crisis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), which threatens both animal and human medicine.

Training immune cells early

Working with primary chicken immune cells and cell lines, the research team traced how sodium butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid naturally produced by gut bacteria, acts as an immune system programmer. By exposing developing immune cells, called macrophages, to this compound, the researchers successfully trained the chickens' natural immune defenses to fight future infections.

The study found that these reprogrammed chicken immune cells showed a dramatic increase in their ability to kill a wide range of dangerous bacteria, including multiple strains of E. coli, Salmonella, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus.

Crucially, the research found a time frame within which the immune reprogramming takes place. The immune system upgrade only occurs if the molecule is introduced during the early, plastic stages of the immune cells' development. When applied to fully mature cells, the treatment failed to improve their disease-fighting capabilities, providing vital clues for how this method must be timed in real-world farming.

A non-inflammatory attack route

Unlike traditional immune training agents that cause high levels of tissue-damaging inflammation, sodium butyrate works through an alternative route. It encourages cells to use a precise two-pronged internal attack: boosting the production of destructive oxygen molecules (reactive oxygen species) and accelerating "autophagy," a cellular self-cleaning process that traps and digests invading germs.

Shahriar Behboudi, professor of immunology at the Bristol Veterinary School and senior author of the study, said, "Our findings suggest that trained immunity exists along a much wider spectrum of phenotypes than previously thought.

"By demonstrating that a natural gut metabolite can program immune cells through an alternative, non-inflammatory axis, we open up exciting new possibilities for enhancing animal health naturally, without the collateral damage of excessive inflammation."

Dr. James Adams, a research fellow in the School of Veterinary Medicine at the University of Surrey and the first author of the paper, added, "The increasing spread of diseases among chickens is of great concern. Bacterial diseases cause significant animal health and welfare issues in poultry, incurring devastating economic losses and potential disruption to our food chain.

"Antimicrobial resistance is complicating the management of disease in poultry. Therefore, it is crucial that we develop new ways of controlling bacterial infections in poultry."

A path beyond antibiotics

The study's findings offer a vital framework to help the poultry industry and policymakers design nature-positive farming systems.

As poultry is a major global food source, protecting flocks from disease using natural metabolic compounds is essential for both food security and sustainable development.

The team hopes these findings will pave the way for new gut-health strategies in everyday agriculture, improving animal welfare and reducing the world's reliance on antibiotics.

Publication details

James R Adams et al, Innate immune reprogramming of chicken macrophages by sodium butyrate enhances reactive oxygen species–mediated antimicrobial responses in vitro, The Journal of Immunology (2026). DOI: 10.1093/jimmun/vkag209

content_html_zh:
布里斯托大学领导的研究人员发现了一种天然存在的肠道分子，可以增强鸡对多种细菌感染的免疫反应。 这一进展于今天 8 月 12 日发表在《免疫学杂志》上，为可持续农业和全球抗击抗生素耐药性的斗争迈出了重要一步。

长期以来，保护牲畜免受沙门氏菌和禽致病性大肠杆菌等广泛病原体的侵害一直是农业面临的挑战。 大肠杆菌（APEC），而不严重依赖抗生素。 在农业中过度使用这些药物直接导致全球抗菌素耐药性 (AMR) 危机，威胁到动物和人类医学。

尽早训练免疫细胞

研究小组利用初级鸡免疫细胞和细胞系，追踪了丁酸钠（一种由肠道细菌自然产生的短链脂肪酸）如何充当免疫系统程序员。 通过将正在发育的免疫细胞（称为巨噬细胞）暴露于这种化合物，研究人员成功地训练了鸡的天然免疫防御能力来对抗未来的感染。

研究发现，这些经过重新编程的鸡免疫细胞杀死多种危险细菌（包括多种大肠杆菌菌株）的能力显着增强。 大肠杆菌、沙门氏菌、铜绿假单胞菌和金黄色葡萄球菌。

至关重要的是，该研究发现了免疫重编程发生的时间范围。 只有在免疫细胞发育的早期可塑阶段引入该分子，免疫系统才会升级。 当应用于完全成熟的细胞时，这种治疗方法未能提高它们的抗病能力，这为在现实世界的农业中如何选择这种方法提供了重要线索。

非炎症攻击途径

与导致高水平组织损伤性炎症的传统免疫训练剂不同，丁酸钠通过替代途径发挥作用。 它鼓励细胞使用精确的双管齐下的内部攻击：促进破坏性氧分子（活性氧）的产生并加速“自噬”，这是一种捕获并消化入侵细菌的细胞自我清洁过程。

布里斯托尔兽医学院免疫学教授、该研究的资深作者 Shahriar Behboudi 表示：“我们的研究结果表明，经过训练的免疫力存在的表型范围比之前想象的要广泛得多。

“通过证明天然肠道代谢物可以通过替代的非炎症轴对免疫细胞进行编程，我们为自然地增强动物健康开辟了令人兴奋的新可能性，而不会造成过度炎症的附带损害。”

萨里大学兽医学院研究员、该论文的第一作者詹姆斯·亚当斯博士补充道：“疾病在鸡群中传播的日益严重令人担忧。 细菌性疾病会导致家禽出现严重的动物健康和福利问题，造成毁灭性的经济损失，并可能破坏我们的食物链。

“抗生素耐药性使家禽疾病的管理变得更加复杂。 因此，我们开发控制家禽细菌感染的新方法至关重要。”

超越抗生素的道路

该研究的结果提供了一个重要的框架，帮助家禽业和政策制定者设计对自然有益的农业系统。

由于家禽是全球主要食物来源，因此使用天然代谢化合物保护鸡群免受疾病对于粮食安全和可持续发展至关重要。

研究小组希望这些发现将为日常农业中新的肠道健康策略铺平道路，改善动物福利并减少世界对抗生素的依赖。
